overview: Genome chemistry drives almost everything about a virus's stability, mutation rate, and replication strategy.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Viruses whose genetic material is DNA, single- or double-stranded.
aspects.valueB: Viruses whose genetic material is RNA, single- or double-stranded.

aspects.label: Replication Location
aspects.valueA: Usually replicate in the host cell nucleus, using host DNA polymerase (with exceptions like poxviruses).
aspects.valueB: Usually replicate in the cytoplasm, generally using a virus-encoded RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

aspects.label: Mutation Rate
aspects.valueA: Lower — host DNA polymerases have proofreading ability, giving higher replication fidelity.
aspects.valueB: Higher — most RNA polymerases lack proofreading, leading to rapid mutation and quasispecies formation.

aspects.label: Genome Stability
aspects.valueA: Generally more stable; some can integrate into the host genome (e.g. herpesviruses, HPV).
aspects.valueB: Less stable; retroviruses uniquely convert RNA to DNA via reverse transcriptase before integration.

aspects.label: Examples
aspects.valueA: Herpesviruses, HPV, hepatitis B virus, adenovirus.
aspects.valueB: Influenza virus, HIV, SARS-CoV-2, hepatitis C virus.

aspects.label: Implication for Vaccines/Drugs
aspects.valueA: Antigenic stability makes long-lasting vaccines more feasible.
aspects.valueB: High mutation rate drives antigenic drift/shift, requiring frequently updated vaccines (e.g. seasonal flu).

aspects.label: Common Detection Methods
aspects.valueB: RT-PCR, which requires an added reverse transcription step before amplification.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: DNA genome, replicated with high fidelity, usually in the nucleus.
aspects.valueB: RNA genome, replicated with low fidelity, usually in the cytoplasm.
